title: The other half
hook: Aristophanes' myth: humans split in two, searching for their other half (Symposium 189–193)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diotima's staircase. Your line was the ladder. Did something beautiful lift you a step? Today, the same dinner party, and a very different speech. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

Earlier that night at the Symposium, before Socrates speaks, it's the comic playwright Aristophanes' turn, and he has the hiccups. A doctor at the table tells him to hold his breath, then to gargle with water, and if all else fails, to tickle his nose and sneeze. The doctor speaks in his place while he recovers. When Aristophanes finally gets the floor, he tells the strangest story of the evening, and maybe the easiest one to remember.

First, round people. Long ago, Aristophanes says, humans were round, with four arms, four legs and two faces looking opposite ways. When they ran, they rolled along like tumblers turning cartwheels. There were three kinds: male, female, and a kind that was both. Second, cut in two. They grew so strong and bold that they tried to climb up and attack the gods. Zeus didn't wipe them out. He cut each one in half, and Apollo turned their faces around and drew the skin together at the navel, a mark left as a reminder. Third, the search. Ever since, each half longs for its other half. When two find each other, Aristophanes says, they don't want to be apart even for a moment, though neither can say exactly what they want. Love is the name for that desire and pursuit of the whole. Fourth, a comedy, and an answer. It's a playwright's story, told with a wink, and Plato doesn't give it the last word. Later that night, in the speech we heard yesterday, Diotima says love isn't of a half or a whole unless it is good. Still, the picture has lasted. Some readers hear in it something they know: meeting a person and recognizing them.
screen: `ROUND PEOPLE.` · `CUT IN TWO.` · `THE SEARCH.` · `A COMEDY, AND AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `THE OTHER HALF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who completes something in you: a partner, a friend, a sister or brother, a teacher, someone who supplies what you lack. It doesn't have to be romance. Breathe in and let their face come. Breathe out and notice one thing they bring that you don't. Stay with that for a while, without needing to explain it. After the sit, if you'd like, send them a short thank you, a sentence or two, nothing grand. The bell holds the time.
The other half. Aristophanes' myth in the Symposium: people cut in two, each half searching for the other, and love as the pursuit of the whole. Today's word.
Your line: the half. Today, thank the person who came to mind, and tell them one thing they bring that you don't. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Aristophanes' myth from Plato's Symposium is read in philosophy and literature classes, and its picture of searching for one's other half turns up in writing about love; readers take it as comedy, as a myth, or both.

fork.setup: you're Zeus. the round people are so strong they're trying to attack the gods. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he cuts each one in half, and ever since, each half has gone looking for the other.

trapdoor: what you thought: soulmates, the one person made for you.
what it means: a comic myth: round humans cut in two by Zeus, each half searching, love the pursuit of the whole.
what a scholar hears: Plato gives the myth to a comic playwright, then has Diotima answer it: love isn't of the half unless the half is good.

notes: All of Plato paraphrased. 'Desire and pursuit of the whole' echoes Jowett's wording at 192e; unquoted here. Confirm.
The doctor is Eryximachus; his remedies (hold breath, gargle, sneeze) at 185d–e. Confirm he speaks in Aristophanes' place.
Three kinds (male, female, androgynous) at 189d–e; the navel as a reminder at 190e–191a. Confirm.
Diotima's reply at 205d–e is phrased loosely ('love isn't of a half or a whole unless it is good'); confirm.
The myth concerns same-sex as well as opposite-sex pairs; the script keeps the practice open to any kind of bond.

Audit: no changes. Hiccups and Eryximachus's remedies, round people (four arms, four legs, two faces, cartwheels), three kinds, the attack on the gods, Apollo and the navel, and Diotima's reply at 205e all checked against the text.
